Florence, August. The family wants to make Karl a partner in the trattoria. Karl has to give a short speech and shows it to Bianca, who corrects it.
Listen to the beginning: “Dear friends, today I made an important decision.”
Nice, but in Italian a decision isn’t made: it’s taken. “Ho preso una decisione.”
Like a bus. In Romanian too, Matei told me, a decision is taken. English, on the other hand, makes it.
All right. Then I say: “I ask you to pay attention.”
No, that’s pure English. Attention isn’t paid, it’s lent. “Vi chiedo di prestare attenzione.”

An exam is sat, or given. And if you succeed, you pass it. “Quando ho sostenuto l’esame.”
So Italian words don’t go with whoever they like. They have fixed friends.
Exactly. They’re called collocations. You don’t learn them with grammar, but by listening. Like Grandma’s recipes.

A collocation is a combination of words that native speakers always use together. Grammatically, other combinations would be possible too, but they sound “foreign”. There is no rule: you learn them as blocks.

On 12 July, in the middle of that July full of new words, letters to the Crusca and prototypes at the Uffizi, Pietro had turned sixteen. Almost nobody had remembered in time. Not out of meanness: simply, too many things were happening that month. Graziella had just returned to the kitchen after the operation, Davide spent his days at the museum, Viola was waiting for the Crusca’s reply, and the trattoria was full of tourists from morning to night. Pietro himself had almost forgotten. He only realised in the evening, when Sara, his mother, came up to the old children’s room, the one that was now Viola’s, with a pencil and a tape measure. On the door frame were all the notches: those of his father Marco, from 1978 to 1991, and next to them Pietro’s, one for every birthday, and lower down Viola’s. Pietro leaned against the frame, barefoot, and Sara drew the line. One metre eighty-four. His father, at sixteen, had reached one metre seventy-nine.

Marco came home from the hospital at ten in the evening, dead tired after a twelve-hour shift, and found his son and his wife sitting on the floor of Viola’s room, in front of the door frame, comparing the notches with a torch. He sat down with them. For a while nobody spoke. Then Marco touched his own sixteen-year notch, a crooked line drawn by Graziella in 1991, with the date written beside it in Aldo’s handwriting. “That day your grandfather told me something,” he said. “He told me that at sixteen a man stops growing in height and starts growing in another direction.” Pietro asked which one. Marco thought about it. “He didn’t explain,” he said. “He said I’d realise it by myself.” And did you?, Pietro asked. His father laughed softly, so as not to wake Viola. “It took me twenty years,” he replied. “I hope it takes you less.” Then he took a small package out of the pocket of his white coat: it was a red penknife, with Aldo’s A engraved on the handle. It had been his father’s. Now it was Pietro’s.

Only one person, that day, had remembered the birthday since the morning. Bianca had arrived at the trattoria at eleven, with a rectangular parcel wrapped in newspaper, and had given it to him without ceremony, between one table to lay and the next. Inside was a big, heavy book with a blue cover: a dictionary of collocations. Pietro didn’t even know such a thing existed. He opened it at random and read: “Decisione: prendere, adottare, rimandare, revocare una decisione; una decisione sofferta, affrettata, irrevocabile.” Bianca explained that an ordinary dictionary tells you what a word means, but this one tells you who it goes with. “Words are like people,” she said. “It isn’t enough to know their names. You have to know who they hang out with.” On the first page there was a dedication, in her small, neat handwriting: “To Pietro, who asks too many questions. Here are the answers nobody can explain. B.” Pietro put it on his bedside table, next to the black notebook. That night he read it until two, like a novel.

In August, for the first time since 1966, the trattoria closed for two whole weeks. Dr Neri had decided it, not Graziella. At the check-up at the end of July the cardiologist had told her, with his usual calm, that her heart was fine, but that a person operated on in May could not work fourteen hours a day in August in a kitchen at forty degrees. Graziella had protested. She had said that in fifty-five years she had never closed, not even for her wedding, not even when Aldo died. Dr Neri had let her talk, then written something on a sheet of paper and given it to her. It was a prescription. It said: “Two weeks of absolute rest. No kitchen. No customers. One walk a day, preferably with a grandchild.” Graziella had read it three times. Then she had folded it in four and put it in her apron, next to the Crusca’s letter. That evening, at dinner, she had announced the closure in the tone of someone announcing a military defeat.

The closure, though, raised a question nobody had foreseen. After the operation, on lawyer Bardi’s advice, Graziella had turned the trattoria into a small family company, so that if something happened to her nobody would be left without work. There were five partners, and they had signed the deed before the notary at the end of June: Graziella, Marco, Sara, Matei and Giulia. And then there was Karl, who for months, before going to the workshop at the Ernesto cooperative, had come into the kitchen every morning at five, who knew the ribollita recipe better than anyone except Graziella, who had sworn to keep the secret of the nepitella, but who for the trattoria was nothing: neither relative, nor employee, nor partner. It was Giulia who raised the question, one evening, on the terrace. “Karl has been getting up at five for months to learn a soup that one day he’ll make himself,” she said. “And for the trattoria he doesn’t exist. It isn’t fair. Karl isn’t a guest. He’s one of us.” Graziella said nothing. But the next day she phoned the notary. And the following week she called an extraordinary meeting of the partners for the fifteenth of August, Ferragosto, on the terrace in via della Chiesa, with a single item on the agenda.

The item on the agenda was: “Admission of a new partner.” Karl discovered it by chance, reading the notice pinned up in the kitchen, and went pale. He went to Graziella with the sheet in his hand and asked her if it was a joke. Graziella, sitting in her armchair with her feet on a stool as the doctor had ordered, replied that notaries never joke. Then she explained the rules: on the day of the meeting, before the vote, the candidate had to give a short speech to the partners, to explain why he wanted to join the company. Five minutes, no more. In Italian, of course. Karl sat down on the edge of the sofa. He had spoken Italian every day for years, in the workshop, in the kitchen, at the market. But a speech was something else. A speech had to be perfect. That night he didn’t sleep. He wrote three versions, tore up all three, and at five in the morning, instead of going to make the ribollita, which wasn’t being made that day, he went and knocked on Bianca’s door.

Bianca opened the door in her pyjamas, with her hair in a mess, and looked at him the way you look at a ghost. Karl showed her the sheet. Bianca read it on the doorstep, yawning, and by the third line she had stopped yawning. The speech was moving. Karl told his story: the fishing village in Malta, his mother who painted eyes on the boats, the years as an apprentice restorer in Malta and then in Rome, the interview in Florence, the first time he had tasted Graziella’s ribollita, one rainy evening, with no money in his pocket. But it was full of mistakes. Not grammar mistakes: Karl knew grammar better than many Italians. They were subtler mistakes, harder to see. The words were all correct, but they went together in the wrong way. “Ho fatto una decisione.” “Vi chiedo di pagare attenzione.” “Quando ho preso il mio esame.” “In quel giorno ho fatto molti amici.” Bianca let him in, put the moka on the stove and said: “Sit down. I’ll explain what a collocation is.”

She explained that in every language certain words go together out of habit, like old friends who always sit at the same table. There is no logical rule. In Italian a decision is taken, not made. Attention is lent, not paid. An exam is sat, or given, and if it goes well it is passed. Friends aren’t made: you make them for yourself, “mi sono fatto degli amici”. Rain, when it is heavy, is pouring. Hunger, when it is great, is wolfish. And someone who is very tired isn’t “very tired”: he is dead tired. Karl listened and took notes, that is, as Bianca pointed out to him, he did something that in Italian is “taken” even though it isn’t carried off. Then he asked where his mistakes came from. Bianca looked at the sheet again. “From English,” she said. “You think in Maltese, translate into English and then into Italian. And English leaves its fingerprints on you.” Karl was silent. Then he laughed. “Like Totò’s T,” he said. “A fingerprint you can’t see, but it’s there.”

They worked on the speech for three days. Bianca didn’t rewrite anything: she said the speech had to remain Karl’s, with his voice, with his way of telling things. She corrected only the collocations, one by one, explaining the reason each time, or admitting there was no reason. “Why do you say prendere freddo and not prendere caldo?” Karl asked. “I don’t know,” Bianca replied. “That’s how it’s said.” “Why do you dare retta to someone, but not dare ascolto?” “You can dare ascolto too, actually. But retta is more common.” “And why do you fare colazione but prendere un caffè?” Bianca raised her hands. “Karl, if I knew, I’d be teaching at the university.” Karl laughed and said that in that case Italian was like Graziella’s cooking: there were rules, but the real rules weren’t written anywhere, you learned them only by standing next to the stove. Bianca nodded. “That’s why you’re perfect for the trattoria,” she said. “You learned both things in the same way.”

The day before the meeting, Karl rehearsed the speech in the workshop, in front of a small but strict audience: Matei, Chiara and Davide, sitting on stools among the easels. He recited it all without getting a single collocation wrong, and at the end Chiara applauded. Matei, on the other hand, stayed thoughtful. Then he told them that he too, in his first months in Florence, had made mistakes of that kind, but from Romanian. One July afternoon he had come into the trattoria sweaty, sat down at the counter and said to Graziella: “Sono caldo.” In Romanian that’s more or less how you say it: mi-e cald. But in Italian “sono caldo” doesn’t mean you feel hot: it means you yourself are hot, like a stove, or worse, like someone in love. Graziella had burst out laughing so loudly that the customers turned round. Then she had brought him a glass of cold water and said: “You say ho caldo, my boy. Heat is something you have, not something you are.” Davide asked whether Matei had been upset. Matei smiled. “Not at all,” he said. “That day I understood that in that trattoria I was allowed to make mistakes. And that’s where I started to really learn.”

Meanwhile Graziella, forced to rest, was bored to death. For the first time in her life she had her days free, and she didn’t know what to do with them. On the first day she cleaned the whole house, until Giulia took the cloth out of her hand. On the second day she tidied the drawers, and found things she hadn’t seen for forty years. On the third day, obeying Dr Neri’s prescription, she began taking a walk every day with a grandchild. Since her real grandchildren were busy, she made do with the adopted ones: one day Viola, one day Davide, one day Pietro. With Viola she went to the Boboli gardens, where the little girl taught the word abbraccioso to a family of Dutch tourists. With Davide she went to the Uffizi, to see the Lippina in relief, and she touched it too, with her eyes closed, and said the angel really was laughing. With Pietro, on the fourth day, she went to a place she hadn’t been back to for many years. She didn’t tell him where. She only told him to put on comfortable shoes, because the road went uphill.

The road climbed towards San Miniato al Monte, the white and green church that overlooks Florence from the other side of the Arno. Graziella walked slowly, leaning on Pietro’s arm, and stopped at every bend to catch her breath. Pietro asked her several times whether she wanted to turn back. She always said no, in the tone of someone who has taken a decision and has no intention of changing it. When they reached the top, they didn’t go into the church. Graziella took him round the back, into the little cemetery, among the old tombs and the cypresses, to a simple slab of grey marble, with a name and, beneath it, two dates: “Aldo”, and below “1948 – 2013”. Pietro had never been there. He knew his grandfather was buried there, but Graziella had never brought him. She said the dead are where you remember them, not where you bury them. Now, though, she sat down on the stone bench in front of the grave, took out of her bag a yoghurt pot with a sprig of nepitella in it, and placed it on the slab.

“I’ve come to ask his permission,” said Graziella. Pietro didn’t understand. She explained, looking at the slab and not at him. When she had founded the company, in June, she had made herself a promise: that the trattoria would stay in the family. The partners were her son, her daughter-in-law, and Matei and Giulia, who lived in Aldo’s home and had given her a granddaughter. Karl was something else. Karl had come from outside, with no money, no family, a strange accent and a past nobody knew well. Making him a partner meant breaking that promise. “And I keep my promises,” she said. “Always. It’s the only thing my father taught me.” Pietro was silent. Then he asked her what Grandpa would have said. Graziella smiled for the first time since they had climbed up. “Grandpa?” she said. “Grandpa had come from Bologna with no money, no family, a strange accent. My father had given him a bicycle and a bowl of ribollita. Then he had given him me.”

They stayed sitting on the bench for a long time, while the sun went down behind the hills and the bells of San Miniato rang for vespers. Graziella told Pietro things she had never told him. She told him that Aldo, in the first years, got all the Florentine words wrong, and the customers made fun of him. He said “sfoglia” instead of “pasta”, “tigella” instead of “focaccina”, and once he had asked the fishmonger for a “sardella”, and the fishmonger had made him wait half an hour as a punishment. But Aldo had never taken offence. He listened, corrected himself, learned. After ten years he spoke Florentine better than his father-in-law. After twenty, new customers thought he had been born in San Frediano. “The right words can be learned,” said Graziella. “The right heart can’t. Either you have it or you don’t.” Then she stood up, stroked the slab with her hand, the way you stroke a cheek, and said to Aldo, out loud, as if he were there: “All right then. We’ll make him a partner. But if he gets the ribollita wrong, it’s your fault.”

They came down the hill slowly, by the steps that lead to San Niccolò, with the city lighting up below them, one window at a time. Halfway down Graziella stopped on a step to catch her breath, and Pietro asked her how many promises she had made in her life. She thought about it seriously, counting on her fingers. She said she had made few, because her father had taught her that promises are like debts: the fewer you make, the better you sleep. To her father Renzo she had promised never to close the trattoria, and she had just broken that promise, on Dr Neri’s orders. To Aldo, on their wedding day, she had promised to look after his plant, and she had kept that promise for fifty-four years. And to herself, in June, she had promised to keep the trattoria in the family. “Then you’re not breaking it,” said Pietro. “Karl isn’t coming in from outside. He’s already inside. You let him in yourself, at five in the morning, months ago.” Graziella looked at him for a long time, in the light of the sunset. Then she gave him a light cuff on the back of the head. “You’re too clever,” she said. “You take after your grandfather.”

On Ferragosto Florence was deserted. The Florentines were at the seaside or in the mountains, the shops had their shutters down, and in the streets there were only overheated tourists looking for an open bar. On the terrace in via della Chiesa, however, there was a crowd. The five partners were sitting round the big table, the one with the tablecloth embroidered by Doina, with the notice, the minutes book and a jug of cool water. Around them, standing, were all the others, who had no right to vote but wouldn’t have missed that day for anything in the world: Bellini, Davide and Rita, Bianca, Guido in his abbracciose slippers, signor Franco, Valeria Conti, Mancini with his notepad, and Viola, sitting on the low wall next to Totò’s pot, with a sign she had drawn herself that said “VOTE KARL”. Karl was standing in front of the table, in a pressed white shirt, the sheet with his speech trembling in his hand. Graziella, who as owner was chairing the meeting, banged the wooden spoon on the table three times.

“Go ahead, Mr Borg,” said Graziella, with a formality that made everyone laugh. “You have five minutes.” Karl looked at the sheet. Then, with a gesture Bianca didn’t expect, he folded it and put it in his pocket. He began to speak from memory. “Dear partners, dear friends. A year and a half ago I arrived in Florence from Rome with a suitcase and a job interview. That evening, in pouring rain, I walked into your trattoria soaked to the skin, ravenously hungry and with ten euros in my pocket. Signora Graziella gave me a bowl of ribollita and didn’t let me pay. I asked her why. She answered: because whoever comes in gets fed.” He paused. Nobody spoke. “That evening,” he went on, “I took a decision. I decided I wanted to learn to make that soup. Not to sell it. So that I too, one day, could give it to someone who comes in soaked to the skin with ten euros in his pocket.”

Karl spoke for four and a half minutes. He told them about the five o’clock mornings, the first mistakes, the burnt garlic Graziella had made him throw away three times in a row, the day she had told him “brava” for the first time, in the feminine, by mistake, and he hadn’t corrected her because he was too happy. He talked about the nepitella, without saying what it was, only that he had sworn to keep a secret and would keep it whatever happened. He didn’t get a single collocation wrong. He said he had taken a risk coming to Florence, and had never regretted it. He said he had made many mistakes, but that in that kitchen mistakes were corrected, not punished. He said he was asking the partners to take a difficult decision, and that whatever decision they took, he would respect it, and the next morning he would be in the kitchen at five anyway. Then he looked at Graziella. “I promised never to write the recipe down,” he said. “And I kept my promise. Now I promise you something else: to teach it, one day, to whoever comes after me.”

When Karl finished, there was a long silence. Then Graziella opened the minutes book, picked up the pen and said in an official voice: “We will now proceed to the vote. Those in favour of admitting Mr Karl Borg as a partner in the trattoria raise your hand.” She raised her hand first. Then Matei and Giulia raised theirs, together, as they did everything. Then Marco. Then Sara, who was crying and laughing at the same time. Five hands out of five. Graziella wrote in the minutes, slowly, in her crooked handwriting: “Approved unanimously.” Then she looked up and said to Karl: “Welcome, partner.” The terrace exploded. Viola jumped down from the wall waving her sign and ran to hug Karl round the legs, shouting that he was abbraccioso. Guido threw a slipper into the air. Mancini wrote so fast that he broke his pencil. Karl stood motionless, his arms by his sides, unable to say a word. It was Bianca who said it for him. “He gave a perfect speech,” she said. “He didn’t get anything wrong.” Karl shook his head. “One thing,” he said. “I said ‘dear partners’. I should have said ‘dear family’.”

Before the party began, Bellini asked to speak. Graziella granted it, reminding him that he wasn’t a partner and therefore had two minutes, not five. Bellini laughed and said one would be enough. He raised his glass to Karl and told them that Ernesto, his grandfather, in 1946, had taken into his workshop a boy from Prato who had neither money nor family, because the war had taken everything from him. That boy was called Giovanni, and he had become one of the best gilders in Florence. When people asked him why he had taken him on, Ernesto always gave the same answer: “Because he had the right hands and his heart in the right place. The rest can be learned.” Bellini looked at Graziella. “It seems to me,” he said, “that this family keeps making the same choice, eighty years later. You took a risk, and you were right to take it.” Then he took a sip, sat down and added, turning to Karl, with a smile: “And now that you’re a partner, make sure you don’t take too many liberties with the garlic.” Everyone burst out laughing, Karl first.

They partied until late. Since the trattoria was closed and Graziella wasn’t allowed to cook, everyone else cooked, each a dish from their own land, on the little stove on the terrace and in Giulia’s kitchen. Karl made his mother’s pastizzi, with ricotta and peas. Matei made mici, which Ion had taught him to make over the phone. Rita brought her mother’s Sardinian culurgiones. Guido brought a tart bought from a pastry shop, confessing that he couldn’t cook anything, but that he knew how to choose pastry shops well, which was a talent anyway. Graziella, sitting in her armchair like a queen, tasted everything and gave marks, and nobody got more than seven, except the pastizzi, which got eight. Karl said that an eight from Graziella was worth more than any diploma. Towards midnight, when everyone was dead tired and the moon was high above the bell tower of Santo Spirito, Pietro noticed that Davide was sitting alone in a corner, on the low wall, with his sketchbook closed on his knees. He went and sat down next to him.

Davide told him he was happy for Karl, but that that evening he had been thinking about something. Karl had found his place. He had a word to say what he was: partner. Pietro had one too, in a way: writer, or journalist, or whatever he would become with his black notebook. But he, Davide, didn’t know what to call himself. He wasn’t a restorer, because he didn’t restore. He wasn’t an artist, because he didn’t invent. He wasn’t a technician, because he didn’t print anything. He did something that had no name: he took a painting made for the eyes and turned it into something for the hands. “At the museum they call me ‘the consultant’,” he said. “But it’s an empty word. It doesn’t mean anything.” Pietro smiled. It was the right moment, the one he had been waiting for for three weeks. He took out of his pocket Aldo’s red penknife and a note folded in two. On the note, in his neatest handwriting, a single word was written.

The word was: “tattigrafo”. Davide read it twice, moving his lips. Then he asked what it meant. Pietro explained it the way Bianca had taught him, taking it apart into pieces. Tatto, the sense of the hands. Plus -grafo, from Greek, the one who writes or draws, as in fotografo, geografo, calligrafo. The photographer writes with light. The geographer writes the earth. The tattigrafo writes for touch. “It’s a well-formed word,” said Pietro, with the air of an academician of the Crusca. “I checked. It doesn’t exist anywhere. It’s yours, if you want it.” Davide looked at the note for a long time without saying anything. Then he opened his sketchbook at the first page, where his name was written, and underneath, in pencil, he wrote: “tattigrafo”. He looked at it. Then he went over it in pen, because pencil rubs out. “Now I have to give it to as many people as I can,” he said, repeating the linguist’s sentence. “Otherwise it’s worth nothing.” Pietro nodded. “Start tomorrow,” he said. “At the museum. Say you’re Italy’s first tattigrafo.”

Then Pietro gave him the red penknife too. Davide refused it at once: he knew whose it had been, and he knew Marco had given it to Pietro for his sixteenth birthday. But Pietro insisted. He explained that he wasn’t giving it to him: he was lending it. Forever, maybe, but lent. “My grandfather gave my grandmother a loaf of bread in sixty-six,” he said. “Your grandfather shovelled mud in San Frediano. Ernesto gave a brush to Aldo. Bellini gave a brush to Matei. Here things pass from hand to hand. That’s how it works.” Davide took the penknife and turned it between his fingers, in the moonlight. Aldo’s A, engraved on the handle, was almost worn away. “And what do I do with it?” he asked. Pietro shrugged. “Sharpen your pencils,” he said. “A tattigrafo needs sharp pencils.” Davide laughed, for the first time that evening. Then, without saying anything, he hugged him, quickly and clumsily, the way boys hug at that age, and stood up abruptly, as if embarrassed. Viola, on the wall, pretending to sleep, shouted: “Abbraccioso!”

Later, when everyone had gone and the terrace was full of dirty plates, empty glasses and pastizzi crumbs, Pietro helped Graziella down the stairs to the old home above the trattoria. She stopped in front of Viola’s room; Viola was asleep with the “VOTE KARL” sign clutched in her arms. She switched on the little light in the corridor and looked at the door frame, with all the notches: Marco, Pietro, Viola. Then she took a pencil out of her apron pocket and told Pietro to lean against the frame. Pietro reminded her that they had already made the sixteen-year notch, on 12 July. Graziella shook her head. “Not that one,” she said. “Another one.” Pietro leaned back. Graziella didn’t draw a line above his head. She drew it at the height of his heart. Then she wrote beside it, very small: “15 August. He understood.” Pietro asked what he had understood. Graziella looked at him the way she used to look at him when he was five and asked too many questions. “That you also grow in another direction,” she replied. “Your father told me. And your grandfather had told him.”
